title: Check Land Records Online 2026: Bhulekh, Khasra, Bhu Naksha
meta_description: Check land records on web free: every state's Bhulekh portal verified for 2026. Khasra, khatauni, jamabandi, Bhu Naksha maps, plus the Telangana switch.

hero.one_liner: Check land ownership, khasra/khatauni records, plot maps, and property history online for FREE - every state has a digital Bhulekh portal with verified records

sections.heading: What Land Records Tell You Before Anyone Else Will
content: Land records on the web show who owns a plot, its exact area, its type, and its transaction history, all from government revenue registers. Five minutes on your state's portal answers questions a seller might dance around for weeks.
Every state runs its own free portal, usually called Bhulekh, and none of them needs a login for basic viewing. The table below carries every major state's verified portal for 2026.
Before any property advance, any farm loan, or any scheme application, this check comes first. It is the cheapest fraud insurance in India.

This guide covers the verified portal for every major state, the documents by their local names, the mutation process, and the checks that stop fraud. Everything here works on a phone, which is where most of these checks happen.

sections.title: 📌 Telangana Changed Portals: Dharani Is Gone (Verified August 2026)
sections.content:
Telangana shut down Dharani and replaced it with Bhu Bharati at bhubharati.telangana.gov.in, launched April 2025 under the Bhu Bharati Act and rolled out statewide by June 2025. Old Dharani links no longer serve records.

The new system runs on a unique Bhudhaar ID per land parcel and hands corrections back to Tahsildars. If your saved link says dharani, update it.

sections.title: Watch for Fake Bhulekh Websites
sections.content:
Lookalike sites with names like bhulekh-online or land-records-india charge for records the government gives free, and some harvest personal details. The official portal always ends in .gov.in or .nic.in.

Type the URL from the table above rather than tapping ads in search results. The top ad slot is exactly where fakes live.

sections.heading: Understanding Key Land Record Terms

rows.label: Khasra
rows.value: Village-wise property register listing all plots, owner names, area, and land type. The khasra number uniquely identifies each plot in a village.

rows.label: Khatauni / Khata
rows.value: Consolidated ledger showing one owner's total holdings across plots. Used for tax assessment and revenue collection.

rows.label: Jamabandi
rows.value: The record of rights in northern states like Rajasthan, Punjab, and Haryana, updated in cycles. It is the primary ownership document there, like khatauni elsewhere.

rows.label: Bhu Naksha
rows.value: The digital plot map showing boundaries, dimensions, and neighbouring plots. Lets you visually verify what the text record claims.

rows.label: 7/12 Extract (Satbara)
rows.value: Maharashtra and Gujarat's core document combining ownership and crop details. The single most-requested record in western India.

sections.heading: 5 More Terms That Decide Your Money

items.title: Gata / Survey number
items.sub: The plot's identity from the original survey. Every transaction references it.

items.title: Circle rate
items.sub: District-set minimum registration value. Stamp duty is charged on this even if you paid less.

items.title: Fard / RoR
items.sub: Record of Rights: the most complete document covering ownership, area, type, and encumbrances.

items.title: Encumbrance Certificate
items.sub: Shows loans and mortgages against the property. Non-negotiable before purchase.

items.title: Certified copy
items.sub: Sealed Tehsildar copy that courts and banks accept. Online printouts are information only.

sections.heading: Same Record, Different Name: A Cross-State Decoder
content: India's land records describe the same things under regional names, which trips up anyone dealing across states. The record of rights is jamabandi in Rajasthan, Punjab, and Haryana, khatauni in UP, khatian in Bengal, and pahani in Telangana.

Maharashtra and Gujarat compress ownership plus crop data into the 7/12 extract, called satbara in Marathi. Karnataka's version is the RTC, and Tamil Nadu splits it into patta for ownership and chitta for land classification.

The plot identifier shifts too: khasra in the north, survey number in the south, gata in parts of UP. When a portal asks for a number you do not recognise, it is almost always the same plot ID under a local name.

sections.heading: Bhu Naksha: Reading the Map Like a Buyer
content: Bhu Naksha is the cadastral map layer on most Bhulekh portals. Enter the khasra or survey number and the plot renders with its boundaries, dimensions, and every neighbouring plot number.
Three things to compare: the plot's shape against what you saw on the ground, the computed area against the khasra entry, and the neighbouring plot numbers against what the seller describes.
A plot that looks rectangular on paper but is fenced as an L-shape on site is a boundary dispute waiting to happen. Map mismatches are cheaper to discover before the advance than after registration.

sections.heading: No Khasra Number? Searching by Owner Name
content: Most portals allow owner-name search when the plot number is unknown. Select the village, switch the search mode to name, and type it exactly as revenue records spell it, which often differs from Aadhaar spelling.
Name search throws namesakes in bigger villages, so match the father's name and plot area to isolate the right entry. Once found, note the khasra and khata numbers for every future lookup.
If the name simply does not appear, the land may sit under an ancestor's name with mutation pending, or under a different village's records than assumed. The Patwari resolves both in one visit.

sections.heading: Common Land Record Issues and What Actually Fixes Them
content: Old owner's name still showing: that is a pending mutation. Apply at the Tehsil office with the sale deed and ID proof, and the record updates after approval.
Online record differs from the Tehsil register: the physical record wins. Recent mutations can take months to reflect online in lagging states, so get a certified copy for anything that matters.
Agricultural land you want for a house: construction needs land conversion through the District Collector first. It takes months and can be refused, so verify land type before buying, not after.
Disputed or court-case tags: ask the Patwari what the case is, and walk away unless it resolves in the seller's favour. Discounted disputed land is how buyers lose everything.
Mortgage on the property: the Encumbrance Certificate reveals it. The seller clears the loan and produces the bank's NOC before registration, or the deal does not happen.

sections.heading: 🔄 Mutation (Dakhil Kharij): Start to Finish

items.desc: Registered sale deed or succession certificate, ID proof, and the state's fee of roughly ₹50-200. Many states now accept the application on the Bhulekh portal itself.
The village revenue officer checks the deed against existing records. Objections from other claimants are invited in this window.
The Tehsildar signs off if papers are clean. Contested cases take longer and may need a hearing.
Your name appears in khatauni or jamabandi. Bank loans and scheme benefits like PM Kisan now recognise you as the owner.

sections.heading: Why Mutation Matters More Than People Think
content: Mutation does not create ownership: the registered sale deed does that. Mutation updates the revenue record so the government's books agree with reality.
But unmutated land is practically frozen. Banks refuse loans against it, PM Kisan rejects the application, and the next sale gets complicated.
For inherited land, heirs apply with the death certificate plus a legal heir or succession certificate. Skipping this leaves the deceased's name on record and every benefit stuck in limbo.
Do it within weeks of purchase or inheritance, not years. The fee is small and the queue only grows.

sections.heading: Where Your Land Record Decides the Money
content: PM Kisan pays ₹6,000 a year in three instalments to landholding farmer families, and eligibility is verified straight from state land records. If your name is missing from the khatauni or jamabandi, the application fails regardless of ground reality.
Complete mutation before applying, especially after inheritance. The scheme checks records, not relationships.
Crop loans and KCC: banks want the khatauni in your name, agricultural land type, and no existing mortgage. Certified copies from the Tehsildar carry the weight here.
Home loans on plots need the ownership record, an Encumbrance Certificate, and a conversion order if the land was agricultural. Missing any one stalls the file.
Housing schemes like PM Awas verify land ownership through the same portals. One updated record feeds every application you will ever make.

State schemes ride the same rails: Odisha's KALIA, farm input subsidies, and crop insurance all verify cultivator or owner entries from these records. The pattern never changes: record first, benefit second.

sections.heading: Getting the Encumbrance Certificate
content: The EC comes from the registration department, not the Bhulekh portal, because it tracks registered transactions like mortgages and sales. Most states issue it through their IGRS or registration portal, or at the Sub-Registrar office.
Ask for 30 years of history for a purchase. The fee is modest, typically a few hundred rupees, and delivery ranges from same-day online to a week offline.
A nil-encumbrance EC plus a clean Bhulekh record is the minimum paper floor for any purchase. Banks will independently pull both before sanctioning a loan against the property.

sections.heading: The 7-Point Check Before Any Advance
content: Match the owner name on khatauni with the seller's ID, and the plot area on khasra with the claim. Review mutation history: every past transfer should trace to a registered deed.
Pull the Encumbrance Certificate for 30 years and confirm zero loans. Verify land type suits your use, and check Bhu Naksha boundaries on the ground.
Finally, confirm no disputed or court tags. Due diligence costs roughly ₹6,000-16,000 including a lawyer: about half a percent of a ₹30 lakh purchase, against the risk of losing all of it.

Walk away immediately if the seller cannot show the original sale deed, if the last mutation is incomplete, or if co-owners are absent from the deal. Cheap land with paperwork excuses is expensive land.

sections.title: Online Records Are Not Legal Proof
sections.content:
The online khatauni, jamabandi, or 7/12 extract is for information only. Courts, banks, and the Sub-Registrar need certified copies with official seal from the Tehsildar office.

Certified copies cost roughly ₹20-100 per page and arrive same-day to a week. Order them early when a transaction is coming.

sections.heading: Why Some States' Portals Lag: The DILRMP Story
content: Digitisation runs under the Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme, and states moved at different speeds. That is why Karnataka's Bhoomi feels seamless while some states still show records months behind the Tehsil register.
When the portal lags, the physical record at the Tehsil office remains the authoritative source. A certified copy from there beats any screenshot.

Telangana's Bhu Bharati rebuild and Punjab's Easy Jamabandi launch show the direction: fewer modules, faster corrections, and unique parcel IDs. Expect more states to relaunch portals over the next few years, which is why bookmarking the table above beats memorising URLs.

sections.heading: What Changed in 2025-26: Portal Shake-Ups Worth Knowing
content: Telangana made the biggest move, retiring Dharani for Bhu Bharati with parcel-level Bhudhaar IDs and Tahsildar-led corrections. Punjab followed with Easy Jamabandi in June 2025, simplifying record access alongside the main jamabandi portal.
Haryana pushed paperless property registration and online demarcation in 2025, tightening the link between registration and revenue records.

The pattern across states is the same: fewer modules, online mutation filing, and digitally signed copies. If your state's portal looks different from last year, it probably relaunched rather than moved.

sections.heading: Checking Family Land From Another City or Abroad
content: Every portal in the table works from anywhere, which makes remote monitoring of ancestral land practical. A quarterly check of the khatauni and Bhu Naksha catches unauthorised mutation attempts early.
For certified copies from a distance, several states courier digitally signed copies, or a relative can collect from the Tehsil with your authorisation letter.

If an unexpected name appears on the record, act immediately through a local lawyer and the Tehsildar. Fraudulent mutations are far easier to reverse within the objection window than after years of silence.

sections.heading: Ordering Certified Copies Without the Runaround
content: Walk into the Tehsildar office with the khasra or khata number, fill the copy application, and pay the per-page fee of roughly ₹20-100. Same-day issue is common for current records, a few days for older years.
Several states now issue digitally signed certified copies straight from the portal, which banks accept. Look for a certified copy or nakal option after the record loads.
Order two copies when a transaction is coming: one for the bank, one for your file. Repeat visits cost more time than the second copy does.

sections.heading: Protecting Your Land From Fraud
content: The classic frauds: forged deeds selling someone else's plot, the same plot sold to two buyers, and government or forest land dressed up as private. Every one of them dies at a five-minute portal check done before the advance.
Insist on the original sale deed, never a photocopy. Pull the 30-year Encumbrance Certificate and hire a lawyer for anything above a few lakh.
After buying: register the deed, complete mutation within 30 days, and keep the original deed in a bank locker with certified copies at home.
If fraud surfaces later, file an FIR, flag the deed with the Sub-Registrar, and pursue recovery in civil court. Speed matters because fraudsters resell fast.

sections.text: Five free minutes on your state's Bhulekh portal is the cheapest property lawyer you will ever hire.

faqs.question: Online land records are not updated. What do I do?
faqs.answer:
Digitization is ongoing in many states - some records may be outdated or lag behind physical records by 3-6 months. For the most current record, visit the Tehsil or Patwari office and get a physical certified copy.

If you've recently bought property, apply for mutation (change of ownership) at the Tehsil office - this updates your name in both physical and online records within 2-4 weeks. For pending mutations, the online portal may not reflect your ownership yet, so always check with the local revenue office.

faqs.question: I want to buy a plot. How do I verify it is not disputed and is free from loans?
faqs.answer:
Step 1: Check land records online (free) for owner name and transaction history. Step 2: Get an encumbrance certificate from the Sub-Registrar office (shows all loans/mortgages on the property for 13-30 years).

Cost: ₹10-50. Step 3: Visit the local Tehsil office and ask the Patwari if there are any court cases or disputes.

Step 4: For high-value purchases (₹50 lakh+), hire a property lawyer to do a title search. Cost: ₹5000-15000.

Only buy after all verifications are clear.

faqs.question: What is mutation and why is it important?
faqs.answer:
Mutation is the official transfer of land ownership in government revenue records after a property changes hands (sale, inheritance, or gift). Without mutation, the old owner's name remains in records.

This means: Government benefits (PM Kisan, etc.) go to the old owner, you cannot use the property as collateral for bank loans, and you may face legal issues if the old owner claims the land again. After buying property, ALWAYS complete mutation at the Tehsil office within 6 months.

Cost: ₹100-500. Time: 2-4 weeks.

faqs.question: Can I check someone else's land records?
faqs.answer:
Yes, land records are public documents. Anyone can check online for free.

Just provide the state, district, village, and plot number or owner name. This is useful for due diligence before buying property.

However, detailed information (exact boundaries, mortgage details) may require in-person visit to Tehsil office with justification (e.g., you're considering buying the land).

faqs.question: What's the difference between khasra and khatauni?
faqs.answer:
Khasra is the plot-wise register listing each individual land parcel with its area and owner. Khatauni is the owner-wise consolidated ledger showing the total land holding of one person across all plots in a village.

Both serve different purposes: Khasra for property identification, Khatauni for tax assessment. You need both documents for property transactions.

faqs.question: How much does a certified copy of land records cost?
faqs.answer:
Certified copies from the Tehsil office cost ₹10-50 per copy, depending on the state and document type. Processing time is 2-5 days.

You need certified copies for property registration, bank loans, and court cases. Online downloads are free but NOT certified - for legal transactions, you must get certified copies with official seal from the revenue office.

faqs.question: I inherited property from my father. How do I update my name in land records?
faqs.answer:
Apply for 'Mutation' at the Tehsil office. You'll need: (1) Your father's death certificate, (2) Your ID proof (Aadhaar/PAN), (3) Copy of the original land record showing your father's name, (4) An affidavit on stamp paper stating you're the legal heir.

Cost: ₹200-500 depending on property value. Processing: 4-6 weeks.

Once approved, your name appears in the records and you become eligible for government benefits.

faqs.question: Can I sell land without getting a mutation done first?
faqs.answer:
Technically yes: ownership transfers through the registered sale deed, and mutation only updates revenue records. Courts recognise the deed, not the mutation entry.

Practically it is a bad idea. Buyers' lawyers flag unmutated chains, banks refuse loans against such plots, and the sale price suffers.

Complete your mutation first and the sale moves faster.

faqs.question: What is RoR in land records?
faqs.answer:
RoR means Record of Rights: the master document listing owner, area, land type, crop details, and encumbrances for a plot. States call it fard, jamabandi, 7/12, or RTC, but it is the same idea.

It is the single most complete record you can pull, and the one banks ask for first.

faqs.question: Bhu Naksha kaise dekhe online?
faqs.answer:
Open your state's Bhulekh portal from the table above and look for the Bhu Naksha or map option. Select district, tehsil, and village, then enter the khasra or survey number.

The plot map loads with boundaries and neighbouring plots. Match the shape and area against the text record and the ground before any deal.

faqs.question: Is Dharani still working in Telangana?
faqs.answer:
No. Telangana replaced Dharani with Bhu Bharati at bhubharati.telangana.gov.in, launched in April 2025 and statewide by June 2025.

Land records, Pahani, and mutations now run through Bhu Bharati with a unique Bhudhaar ID per parcel. Old Dharani bookmarks should be updated.

faqs.question: Mutation me kitna time lagta hai?
faqs.answer:
A clean mutation typically clears in 2-4 weeks after application at the Tehsil, covering Patwari verification and the Tehsildar's approval. Contested cases with objections take longer.

Fees run roughly ₹50-200 depending on state, and many portals now accept the application online. Track status on the same Bhulekh portal.

disclaimer: Land records are for reference and verification. For legal property transactions, always obtain certified copies from the respective District Tehsil/Revenue office. This guide reflects processes as of March 2026. Procedures, portal URLs, and fees may vary by state. Always verify directly with your state's revenue department for latest information.
